questionText: A headline reads: “Generative AI touches 60% of office tasks.” Which quantity does it measure?

answerOptions.text: A forecast of jobs that will disappear
Task exposure: overlap of the technology with tasks
A measured employment effect after deployment
The share of firms already using generative AI

explanation: “Touches” describes overlap with tasks. The figure says nothing about jobs, deployment or effects.

questionText: What does the IAB's substitution potential describe?

answerOptions.text: How many jobs in an occupation will disappear by 2030
How many firms have already automated an occupation
Which share of core tasks could in principle be automated with today's technology
How satisfied employees are with AI tools

explanation: The IAB works with market-ready technology and stresses that substitutability does not mean automation actually happens.

questionText: How do you find out whether an AI tool saves your team time?

answerOptions.text: Measure the same task with and without the tool, including review and correction time
Take the time saving from the vendor's data sheet
Treat the share of high exposure in the task profile as the saving
Ask the team for their impression after one day

explanation: Only a comparison against a baseline shows the benefit. Leaving out review time overstates the saving.

questionText: A tool counts how quickly employees close tickets. What does Section 87(1) no. 6 BetrVG provide for this?

answerOptions.text: Each employee's individual consent replaces the works council
The employer may introduce such tools without involving anyone
Only tools that use AI are subject to co-determination
The works council co-determines technical systems intended to monitor behaviour or performance, unless a statute or collective agreement settles the matter

explanation: The right belongs to the works council, not the individual. Whether a system is covered depends on function and use, not on the AI label.

questionText: A viral video has no Content Credentials. What follows?

answerOptions.text: It has been manipulated
Nothing conclusive: you must check source, origin and context in other ways
It is genuine because there is no AI label
It must not be reported

explanation: Platforms often strip metadata on upload. Missing credentials prove neither manipulation nor authenticity.

questionText: A post claims “bridge collapse in Exampletown last night”. A reverse search finds the same video from 2021 in another place. What is the result?

answerOptions.text: A deepfake, because the details are wrong
Not verified, because no detector was used
The claim is refuted: genuine footage in a false context
Supported, because the video is genuine

explanation: What gets checked is the claim. Genuine footage with a false time and place refutes it, no AI involved.

questionText: A detector catches 92% of fakes and wrongly flags 8% of genuine items. Only 1% of the checked items are fake. Roughly how often is an alert right?

answerOptions.text: About one time in ten
92% of the time
99% of the time
50% of the time

explanation: Per 1,000 items: about 9 correct alerts against about 79 false alarms. When fakes are rare, false alarms dominate.

questionText: Which statement about a deepfake detector's percentage is correct?

answerOptions.text: A “real” result proves authenticity
From 90% a piece of content legally counts as a deepfake
The number is always the probability that this exact item is fake
It is a model-dependent estimate that depends on training data, compression and threshold

explanation: Detector scores are not automatically calibrated. They are at most an additional hint alongside provenance and context.

questionText: What does Article 16 of the Digital Services Act require of hosting services?

answerOptions.text: To delete every reported item within 24 hours
An easily accessible notice procedure and timely, diligent, non-arbitrary and objective processing of notices
To pass every notice on to the police
To screen all uploads for deepfakes in advance

explanation: Article 16 governs the notice procedure. The platform must process and decide, but need not remove every item.

questionText: An AI-altered photo of you is shared publicly without your consent. Which provision is the starting point?

answerOptions.text: Article 16 DSA alone, because image rights do not apply online
Section 87 BetrVG
Section 22 KUG: images of a person may only be shared with consent; exceptions under Section 23 KUG need checking
Section 22 KUG also protects your voice in every recording

explanation: Section 22 KUG protects a person's image. For the voice alone, personality rights and data protection law may apply.

questionText: What did the Gender Shades study (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018) find?

answerOptions.text: In gender classification the highest error rate for lighter-skinned men was 0.8%, for darker-skinned women up to 34.7%
Face recognition identifies all groups equally well
The cause was proven to lie in each vendor's training data
The systems misidentified individual people

explanation: The study measured binary gender classification, not identification. It establishes the gap in the study design, not the cause for each vendor.

questionText: A vendor reports 98% overall accuracy. Why is that not enough?

answerOptions.text: Because 98% falls below a statutory minimum accuracy for AI systems
Because accuracy is only meaningful for test sets of more than 10,000 images
Because the overall figure always reflects the error rate of the largest group
Because an overall figure can hide a high error rate in a group that is rare in the test set

explanation: The overall figure depends on the make-up of the test set. Only error rates per group show who the errors hit.

questionText: Two groups have different base rates and prediction is imperfect. What did Chouldechova (2017) and Kleinberg et al. (2016) show?

answerOptions.text: With enough data, all fairness measures can be met at once
Equal error rates and equal meaning of a flag generally cannot be achieved at the same time
Calibration guarantees equal false alarm rates
Separate thresholds remove every trade-off

explanation: That is the core of the COMPAS debate: ProPublica and Northpointe measured different criteria. People must decide which one counts.

answerOptions.text: Every decision in which any software is involved
A right to the source code of every algorithm
Decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects
Only decisions by public authorities

explanation: If a person genuinely decides, Article 22 does not apply automatically. The right of access under Article 15 still applies.

questionText: From when do the high-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III systems, such as pre-sorting job applications, apply after the amendment by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744?

answerOptions.text: From 2 December 2027
Since 2 February 2025
They never apply to private companies
From 2 August 2030

explanation: Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 the rules for stand-alone Annex III systems apply from 2 December 2027. The GDPR, anti-discrimination law and employment law apply today.
